column4: God says He is “sending the she-camel” (مُرْسِلُوا النَّاقَةِ) as a trial; the camel and the r-s-l word meet explicitly, while God supplies the agent behind its release.

Salih identifies “Allah’s she-camel” as a sign, gives her leave to graze in Allah’s land, and forbids harmful touch; this directly supplies the body, pasture, and protected freedom developed in the section.
Salih again presents Allah’s she-camel as a sign, tells his people to let her eat in Allah’s land, and warns that harming her will bring a near punishment.
Salih assigns the she-camel her own drink (لَهَا شِرْبٌ) and the people theirs on a known day, spelling out the watering right compressed into سُقْيَاهَا.
God orders Salih to announce that the water is divided between them and that each drinking turn must be attended; it completes the trial announced in 54:27.
The people hamstring “the she-camel” (فَعَقَرُوا النَّاقَةَ), defy their Lord’s command, and challenge Salih, joining the exact bodily act to rejection of the messenger.
After “they hamstrung her” (فَعَقَرُوهَا), Salih grants only three days of enjoyment; the verse makes the cut immediately open onto its promised aftermath.
“They hamstrung her” (فَعَقَرُوهَا) and awoke remorseful; the exact act is followed first by inward consequence, before the punishment in 26:158.
The group calls its companion, who reaches out and hamstrings (فَعَقَرَ); this is the fullest parallel to the section’s one rising culprit acting for the collective.
God says He gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign and they wronged her; the surrounding language of sending signs also keeps the camel’s r-s-l association active.
Salih forbids touching the camel with harm and warns of a tremendous day’s punishment; it marks the protected boundary her body is made to cross in 26:157.
Within the camel episode, the believers affirm that Salih is “sent” (مُرْسَلٌ) by his Lord; this identifies the human messenger behind رَسُولُ اللَّهِ and activates the section’s r-s-l camel diction.
“Thamud denied the messengers” (كَذَّبَتْ ثَمُودُ الْمُرْسَلِينَ); the collective formula explains the section’s فَكَذَّبُوهُ as rejection of the messenger whose warning protects the camel.
Salih says, “I am to you a trustworthy messenger” (رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ), giving the same speaker and r-s-l title that the section hears against the easy gait of the camel.

Thamud asks whether it should “follow” (نَتَّبِعُهُ) one human from among them; inside the camel story, their refusal to follow the messenger reverses the section’s young camel naturally following its dam.
The verse tests who “follows the messenger” and who turns “upon his two heels” (عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ); it brings the section’s following, messenger, and bodily heel into one moral fork.
God’s signs were “recited” (تُتْلَىٰ) to them, yet they retreated “on your heels” (عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِكُمْ); both named roots shift from recitation to bodily rearward motion in one verse.

God “raised/sent in every community a messenger” (بَعَثْنَا ... رَسُولًا) and ends by asking for the عَاقِبَة of the deniers; it joins the section’s rising, messenger, denial, and consequence under an explicit divine agent.

The resurrected ask who “raised us from our resting place” (بَعَثَنَا مِن مَرْقَدِنَا), then acknowledge the messengers; unlike the uncaused-looking انْبَعَثَ in the section, this rising explicitly seeks its raiser.

Moses and Aaron say they are two messengers of the Lord and command Pharaoh, “send/release with us” (فَأَرْسِلْ مَعَنَا) Israel; messenger and release occur together as in the section’s untethering explanation.
Muhammad is called a messenger, his possible death or killing is posed, and the hearers may turn “on your heels” (عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِكُمْ); messenger, killed body, and heel become one warning.
“Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?” directs attention to the camel’s made body, the very body whose gait, joints, udder, hock, heel, and rear the section anatomizes.
God gives drink from inside livestock bodies, pure milk between waste and blood (نُسْقِيكُمْ ... لَبَنًا خَالِصًا); it joins the section’s suckling young, udder, animal body, and s-q-y provision.
Livestock are a lesson because God gives drink from what is in their bellies (نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهَا); the animal body itself becomes the source of the watering named beside the she-camel.
Moses finds a whole people watering their flocks while two women hold theirs back; this stages the animal-watering access and restraint implicit in the camel’s allotted drink.
Moses waters the women’s animals for them (فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا), completing the herd-and-water scene opened in 28:23 and supplying a benevolent human agent of s-q-y.
The quake leaves the camel killers fallen motionless in their homes; their prone bodies reverse the animal they first disabled and enact the consequence announced at the harmful touch.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their dwellings, a bodily reversal immediately following their hamstringing of the camel.
The punishment seizes them and the verse calls the episode a sign; it completes the sequence from demanded sign, to wounded camel, to communal consequence.
A single blast leaves them like the dry debris of an enclosure (هِشِيمِ الْمُحْتَظِرِ); the camel trial ends with its keepers reduced to the wreckage of an animal pen.
In the Salih narrative God commands attention to “the aftermath of their plot” (عَاقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ) and says He destroyed them all; it gives the named ع-q-b consequence a collective object.
After Thamud’s defiance and thunderbolt, “they were unable to rise” (فَمَا اسْتَطَاعُوا مِنْ قِيَامٍ); the people’s final incapacity reverses the worst man’s rising toward the camel.

The murdered girl is asked “for what sin” (بِأَيِّ ذَنْبٍ قُتِلَتْ); an innocent female body and ذنب are separated, exposing the guilt of those who kill, as the she-camel’s killers are crushed بِذَنْبِهِمْ.

At the final upheaval, valuable pregnant she-camels are left unattended (الْعِشَارُ عُطِّلَتْ); abandonment reverses the section’s ordinary chain of dam, following young, pasture, and scheduled water.

Sacrificial camel bodies are made among God’s rites, lined up for His name and eaten only after their sides fall; this supplies the lawful, God-directed boundary against attacking Allah’s protected she-camel.

The command “sacrifice” (وَانْحَرْ) supplies the nahr named in the source definition, distinguishing throat-slaughter offered to God from the forbidden hock-cut that the definition says later lent it the name ʿaqr.

Immediately before Salih’s camel scene, God “cut off the last/rear” (قَطَعْنَا دَابِرَ) of sign-deniers; it prefigures the section’s movement from cutting an animal’s rear to erasing a denying people.

After the first human murder, God “sent/raised a crow” (بَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا) to work the earth and teach burial; an animal sent after violence reverses the man who rises in order to violate an animal body.

God disowns human-invented livestock categories including the released sāʾiba; this bounds the section’s release imagery by contrasting fabricated sacred-camel rules with the explicit divine right of Allah’s she-camel.
The arrogant answer the believers, “we disbelieve in what you believe,” giving the immediate communal rejection that turns into bodily assault in 7:77.
After the destruction Salih turns away and says he delivered his Lord’s message (رِسَالَةَ رَبِّي); r-s-l remains audible after the camel’s body and her killers are gone.
When the decree arrives, God saves Salih and the believers by mercy; the verse separates the messenger and hearers of his warning from the consequence following the camel’s injury.
The fallen people are described as though they had never lived there, and Thamud’s denial of its Lord is named; this closes the bodily aftermath begun in 11:65.
Thamud demands a sign from Salih if he is truthful; the she-camel of 26:155 is therefore not incidental livestock but the answer whose body they then test.
“Thamud denied the warnings” opens the compact camel account; it identifies the collective denial that 54:29 concentrates in one companion’s hand.
The people reject the reminder’s being cast upon one man among them and call him a liar; their attack on the selected recipient precedes the divinely selected camel in 54:27.
They are told that tomorrow they will know who is the insolent liar; the promised near disclosure begins the temporal aftermath that the hock-cut triggers.
The question “How were My punishment and warnings?” places the communal stroke directly after the single man’s stroke against the camel.
God says He “sent” Salih to Thamud (أَرْسَلْنَا ... صَالِحًا), after which the people split into contending parties; it supplies the r-s-l agency and divided audience behind the camel warning.
The same Thamud account identifies nine men spreading corruption; without equating them with the cutter, it sets the section’s single worst actor inside an organized corrupt collective.
Their houses stand ruined because of their wrongdoing; it makes the aftermath in 27:51 visible in the very dwellings from which the camel’s communal enemies acted.
God saves those who believed and were mindful; the surviving group marks the boundary within the people whose destruction follows the crime.
Thamud is told to enjoy itself “until a time,” echoing the short respite announced after the camel is hamstrung in 11:65.
They defy their Lord’s command and the thunderbolt seizes them while they look on; it supplies the disobedience and seizure that lead to their inability to stand in 51:45.
Abraham asks God to “raise/send among them a messenger” (وَابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا); it states both sides missing from انْبَعَثَ—a raiser and the one raised—and joins b-ʿ-th to r-s-l.
God favors believers when He “raised among them a messenger” (بَعَثَ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا); divine agency contrasts with the section’s unexpressed instigator of the worst man’s rising.
God is the one who “raised among the unlettered a messenger” (بَعَثَ ... رَسُولًا); the b-ʿ-th and r-s-l camel-derived associations meet in their ordinary Qur’anic mission sense.
God says “then We raised them” (ثُمَّ بَعَثْنَاهُمْ) after the sleepers had lain in the cave; it preserves the section’s two-sided action in which one party causes a resting body to rise.
The sleepers are again said to have been raised so that they question one another; their post-rest movement gives an explicit agent and purpose to b-ʿ-th.

After causing a man to die for a hundred years, God “then raised him” (ثُمَّ بَعَثَهُ), while the surrounding sign also reconstructs his donkey’s bones; bodily raising and animal body are held together.
God takes people by night and “raises you in it” by day (يَبْعَثُكُمْ فِيهِ) until an appointed term; repeated bodily rising is explicitly caused and measured.
A witness “follows it” (يَتْلُوهُ) from God; this uses t-l-w in the spatial sense named by the source’s calf following its dam, now for testimony following proof.
The warned believers may be turned back “on your heels” (عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِكُمْ); it uses ʿaqib in the bodily rear-foot sense supplied by the section’s dictionary note.
The speaker refuses to be returned “on our heels” (عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِنَا) after divine guidance; the physical rear becomes an image of moral reversal rather than a tendon cut from outside.
Satan recoils “on his two heels” (عَلَىٰ عَقِبَيْهِ) when the armies come into view; the named root denotes an enacted backward movement of the foot.
Zechariah calls his wife barren (عَاقِرٌ); the same Qur’anic root that names the camel’s hock-cut here marks a body unable to bear offspring, adding a reproductive edge to the dam-and-young image.
Zechariah says his wife “was barren” (كَانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا); against the source section’s ʿaqr of a limb, this root sense places interruption in the line of offspring.
The question repeats that his wife is barren (امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا); the wonder of a promised child reverses the root’s bodily sense of barrenness, relevant to the camel and following young.

God says earlier generations were destroyed “for their sins” (بِذُنُوبِهِمْ); it repeats the section’s exact causal movement from ذنب to communal destruction while the source dictionary also hears the animal’s rear in the word.
Like Pharaoh’s people and those before them, deniers are seized by God “for their sins” (بِذُنُوبِهِمْ); the formula parallels the reason given for Thamud’s crushing.
Pharaoh’s people and earlier deniers are seized “for their sins” (بِذُنُوبِهِمْ), with God severe in punishment; the same syntax turns guilt into what follows the transgression.
The verse again says earlier peoples denied signs and were destroyed “for their sins” (بِذُنُوبِهِمْ); sign-denial, guilt, and destruction reproduce the camel episode’s causal chain.
“Each We seized for his sin” (فَكُلًّا أَخَذْنَا بِذَنْبِهِ) introduces several bodily forms of destruction, clarifying how a single named guilt can issue in a whole people’s fate.
Former peoples stronger in force and monuments are seized “for their sins” (بِذُنُوبِهِمْ); power does not shield bodies from the consequence attached to guilt.
The camel’s entering a needle’s eye marks an impossible bodily passage; it shifts the animal from vulnerable female body to a measure of size and an absolute boundary.
The condemned drink “like the drinking of thirsty camels” (شُرْبَ الْهِيمِ); uncontrolled thirst reverses the she-camel’s measured, protected drinking turn.
Rain gives drink and grows vegetation “in which you pasture” (فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ); water and grazing appear as one divine provision behind the she-camel’s linked pasture and water rights.
“Eat and pasture your livestock” (وَارْعَوْا أَنْعَامَكُمْ) places human food and animal grazing together within God’s vegetation, matching the protected leave to eat in God’s land.
God brings from the earth “its water and its pasture” (مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَاهَا); the pair names the two provisions assigned to the she-camel.
The water and pasture are provision “for you and your livestock,” making humans and animals joint beneficiaries rather than rivals over the share.
Among the foods God grows are fruit and pasture (أَبًّا); the latter supplies the animal side of the earth from which the she-camel is told to eat.
The growth is provision “for you and your livestock,” again setting human and herd within one apportioned gift.
Subdued livestock provide benefits and drinks (مَشَارِبُ); the question “will they not give thanks?” casts animal provision as a trust, illuminating Thamud’s refusal to honor one animal’s drink.

The Hour makes every nursing female forget what she nurses and every pregnant female drop her load; this catastrophic severing of mother and young contrasts with the section’s calf following and feeding from its dam.

Solomon’s action concerns horses’ shins and necks (بِالسُّوقِ وَالْأَعْنَاقِ), but whether مَسْحًا means stroking or striking is disputed; either reading makes an uncertain yet specific animal-body counterpart to the camel’s hock and later throat.
